question: In a head-on meeting between two power-driven vessels, the navigation rules generally require:
choice_a: The larger vessel to always hold right-of-way regardless of position
choice_b: Neither vessel needs to change course in a head-on meeting
choice_c: Both vessels to alter course to starboard so they pass port to port
choice_d: Both vessels to alter course to port instead
explanation: In a head-on meeting, both power-driven vessels should alter course to starboard so that each passes on the other's port side, resulting in a safe port-to-port passing.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the give-way vessel required to take early and substantial action to avoid collision?
choice_a: The vessel that has the other vessel on its own port side
choice_b: Whichever vessel happens to be larger
choice_c: Whichever vessel is moving faster at the time
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel on its own starboard side
explanation: In a crossing situation, the vessel that has the other vessel on its own starboard side is the give-way vessel and must take early, obvious action to avoid a collision, while the other vessel is generally the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: When one power-driven vessel is overtaking another, which vessel must keep out of the way?
choice_a: The overtaking vessel, regardless of which side it chooses to pass on
choice_c: Neither vessel has any obligation in an overtaking situation
choice_d: Whichever vessel entered the waterway first that day
explanation: The overtaking vessel is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken until it is safely past and clear, no matter which side it passes on.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: When a sailing vessel under sail alone meets a power-driven vessel, which vessel generally has right-of-way?
choice_a: Right-of-way is determined solely by vessel size
choice_b: The sailing vessel is generally the stand-on vessel, and the power-driven vessel must give way
choice_c: The power-driven vessel always has right-of-way over sailing vessels
choice_d: Whichever vessel is closer to shore automatically has right-of-way
explanation: As a general rule, a sailing vessel under sail alone (not under power) is the stand-on vessel and a power-driven vessel must generally give way to it, subject to exceptions such as narrow channels and overtaking situations.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: On the Mississippi River and other Louisiana waters used by large commercial tows, why must recreational boaters give extra clearance to deep-draft vessels confined to a marked channel?
choice_a: Recreational boaters always have right-of-way over commercial traffic regardless of circumstances
choice_b: Large commercial vessels are required to stop for any approaching small craft
choice_c: These vessels have very limited ability to maneuver or stop, and are recognized under the navigation rules as constrained by their draft within a narrow channel
choice_d: Commercial vessels are not required to follow any navigation rules on the Mississippi River
explanation: A vessel constrained by draft, such as a heavily loaded tow confined to a narrow, deep channel on the Mississippi River, has very limited ability to maneuver and cannot simply stop or turn aside, so small craft must give it a wide, early berth.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83, Rule 9 narrow channels), applied to Louisiana's Mississippi River commercial traffic

question: What does it mean for a vessel to be the stand-on vessel in a meeting, crossing, or overtaking situation?
choice_a: It must immediately stop its engines
choice_b: It has no responsibilities at all in the encounter
choice_c: It must always yield, regardless of the situation
choice_d: It should generally maintain its course and speed, while the give-way vessel takes action to avoid collision
explanation: The stand-on vessel should hold its course and speed to remain predictable, allowing the give-way vessel to take clear, early action to avoid a collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: If the stand-on vessel realizes the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action to avoid collision, what should the stand-on vessel do?
choice_a: Take whatever action is necessary, including altering course or speed, to avoid the collision
choice_b: Continue on its original course no matter what, since it legally has the right-of-way
choice_c: Immediately shift into reverse and stop, and take no other action
choice_d: Sound five short blasts and otherwise take no further action
explanation: The stand-on vessel's obligation to hold course and speed is not absolute -- once collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone, the stand-on vessel must take whatever action best avoids the collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: A vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, such as one engaged in dredging operations common on Louisiana's industrial waterways, generally:
choice_a: Has no special status whatsoever under the navigation rules
choice_b: Has right-of-way over most other vessels because of its limited maneuverability
choice_c: Must always yield to recreational vessels nearby
choice_d: Is exempt from all navigation rules while working
explanation: Vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver -- such as those actively dredging, laying cable, or engaged in similar operations -- rank above ordinary power-driven vessels in the right-of-way hierarchy because they cannot readily get out of the way.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83, Rule 18), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: In narrow channels and fairways, such as those found in Louisiana's bayous and ship channels, vessels should generally:
choice_a: Keep to the left (port) side of the channel
choice_b: Ignore channel boundaries entirely when convenient
choice_c: Keep as far to the starboard (right) side of the channel as is safe and practicable
choice_d: Travel down the exact center of the channel at all times
explanation: In a narrow channel, a vessel should keep to the starboard side, allowing safe room for oncoming and passing traffic, particularly important where large commercial vessels also transit the same channel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83, Rule 9), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: What sound signal does a power-driven vessel give when it intends to alter its course to starboard while in sight of another vessel?
choice_c: Five or more short, rapid blasts
explanation: One short blast signals an intent to alter course to starboard; two short blasts signal an intent to alter course to port; three short blasts signal operating astern propulsion.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83, Rule 34), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses

question: Five or more short, rapid blasts of a horn signal what to nearby vessels?
choice_a: Danger or doubt about the other vessel's intentions or actions
choice_b: A routine, friendly greeting between vessels
choice_c: An intention to overtake on the starboard side
choice_d: That the vessel is anchoring for the night
explanation: The danger/doubt signal -- five or more short, rapid blasts -- warns another vessel that its intentions are unclear or that its course of action appears unsafe.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83, Rule 34), standard content across NASBLA-aligned boating courses
